tips: Honey, maple syrup, and molasses all add extra sugar, and sugar makes cold-process soap heat up sharply in the mold. Too much can crack the top, caramelize the center to a deep brown, accelerate trace, or in extreme cases cause a soap volcano.

Keep honey to roughly 1 teaspoon per pound of oils (Soap Queen's recommended rate); treat about 1 tablespoon per pound as an absolute ceiling. In Soap Queen's side-by-side test, a loaf with too much honey still partially gelled in the center even after a full night in the freezer.
Dilute honey in a small amount of warm distilled water so it disperses evenly, then mix it in at light trace rather than into hot lye solution.

Do not insulate a honey or sugar-additive soap. Soap at cooler temperatures (about 100-110 degrees F or below) and place the poured mold in the fridge or freezer for the first 24 hours to keep the color light and prevent overheating.
Expect faster trace and a shorter working window with any sugar additive, so save complicated swirl designs for sugar-free batches or work with a slow-moving recipe.
